title: How a Smartphone Camera Actually Works

youtube.title: How a Smartphone Camera Actually Works (Explained Simply)
youtube.summary: Your phone camera's pixels can't see colour, and it may start shooting before you even tap. In this video we follow light through a phone camera: the lens, the image sensor, how a pixel turns light into a number, the Bayer colour filter and demosaicing, why tiny pixels need pixel binning, and how HDR and night mode stack many frames into one clean photo.
youtube.details:
Key figures (checked November 2026):
- Bayer filter: 50% green, 25% red, 25% blue; Bryce E. Bayer, Eastman Kodak, US patent 3,971,065 (1976)
- Demosaicing estimates about two thirds of the colour data
- Samsung ISOCELL HP3: 200 MP, 0.56 um pixels, 1/1.4-inch; 4-to-1 binning = 50 MP (1.12 um), 16-to-1 = 12.5 MP (2.24 um) (PetaPixel)
- Google HDR+ buffers the latest 9 or 15 frames; Night Sight (2018) captures 6-15 frames, up to 1 s each when still, 1/15 s or less handheld (SlashGear on Google's research)

shorts.headline: Your phone takes photos before you tap
Your camera's pixels can't see colour
How night mode sees in the dark

scenes.chapterTitle: Intro: what happens when you tap
scenes.sub: tiny light sensors on a chip smaller than a fingernail
scenes.text: You point your phone, tap the button, and a sharp, colourful photo appears in a fraction of a second. It feels simple. But inside that tiny camera bump, something remarkable is happening. Some phones now pack two hundred million pixels onto a chip smaller than your fingernail. And here are two surprising facts. First, not one of those pixels can actually see colour. Second, your phone may have started taking photos before you even pressed the button. By the end of this video, you will understand how light becomes a photo, why the pixels are colour blind, and how your phone uses maths to make a picture that a tiny lens should never be able to take.

items.text: A field full of tiny buckets
Rain falls: brighter light, more drops

scenes.text: Let us start with a simple picture. Imagine a huge field covered in millions of tiny buckets, all lined up in a grid. Now it starts to rain. Where the rain falls heavily, the buckets fill up. Where it is only drizzling, they stay almost empty. When the rain stops, you walk along and measure how much water is in each bucket. Write those numbers down in order, and you have a map of where the rain fell. That is almost exactly how a camera sensor works. Each bucket is a pixel. The rain is light. And the numbers you write down become your photo. The brighter a spot in the scene, the more light is collected in that pixel.

scenes.chapterTitle: The parts of a phone camera

items.name: Lens
items.desc: Bends light into a sharp image

items.name: Image sensor
items.desc: A grid of millions of light-sensitive pixels

items.name: Image processor
items.desc: A chip that turns raw numbers into a photo

items.name: Software
items.desc: Combines frames, fixes colour and noise

scenes.text: So what is actually inside the camera bump? There are four main parts. First, the lens. It is a stack of tiny curved pieces of glass or plastic that bend incoming light, so a sharp image lands on the chip behind it. Second, the image sensor. This is the field of buckets, a grid of millions of light sensitive pixels. Third, the image processor, a dedicated chip that turns the raw numbers from the sensor into a picture. And fourth, the software, which combines frames, corrects colours, and cleans up noise. A modern phone camera is honestly half hardware and half maths. Let us follow the light through each step.

scenes.chapterTitle: How a pixel turns light into a number

items.text: They knock loose tiny electric charges
The charge is read out as a number

scenes.text: Light is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. When you take a photo, the lens focuses those photons onto the sensor, which is made of silicon. When a photon hits a pixel, it can knock loose a tiny electric charge inside the silicon. The more light that falls on that pixel, the more charge builds up, just like a bucket filling with rain. When the exposure ends, the sensor reads out the charge from every pixel and converts it into a number. A big number means a bright spot. A small number means a dark one. But notice what is missing. That number only tells you how much light arrived. It says nothing about what colour it was. Every pixel measures brightness only.

scenes.chapterTitle: The Bayer filter: how a sensor sees colour
scenes.text: So how does a colour blind sensor make a colour photo? The trick was invented by a Kodak scientist named Bryce Bayer, and patented in nineteen seventy six. On top of the sensor sits a tiny mosaic of coloured filters, one over each pixel. Each filter lets through only red, only green, or only blue light. So every pixel now measures just one colour. In the Bayer pattern, half of the pixels are green, a quarter are red, and the last quarter are blue. Why so much green? Because Bayer matched the pattern to the human eye, which picks out the most detail in green light. Almost every phone camera today still uses this idea, or a close variation of it.

items.text: Each pixel knows only one colour
It borrows the other two from its neighbours
About two thirds of the colour data is estimated

scenes.text: But wait. If each pixel only knows one colour, how does every pixel in your photo end up with full colour? The answer is educated guessing. A red pixel looks at the green and blue pixels right around it, and borrows their values to estimate the two colours it is missing. Every pixel does the same with its neighbours. That means about two thirds of the colour information in a normal photo was never directly measured. It was calculated. This step is called demosaicing, because it turns the mosaic of single colour pixels into a full colour image. When it goes wrong, you sometimes see strange rainbow patterns on fine stripes, like a checked shirt or a distant fence.

chips.text: Far thinner than a human hair

scenes.text: Now, how small are these pixels? Take one example. Samsung's ISOCELL H P three sensor has two hundred million pixels, and each one is just zero point five six micrometres wide. A micrometre is one millionth of a metre, so each pixel is far thinner than a human hair. And the whole sensor is still smaller than your fingernail. That is an incredible piece of engineering, but it comes with a problem. Remember the buckets in the rain. A tiny bucket catches only a few drops. Smaller pixels catch less light each, and when there is not much light, the random noise in the measurement starts to show up as grain. So how do phones get clean photos from such tiny pixels?

scenes.chapterTitle: Pixel binning: many small pixels act as one
scenes.text: The first answer is called pixel binning. Instead of using every tiny pixel on its own, the phone groups neighbouring pixels together and treats them as one big pixel. It is like pouring four small buckets into one large bucket. On that Samsung sensor, combining four pixels into one gives a fifty megapixel photo with pixels that act like one point one two micrometres wide. Combining sixteen into one gives a twelve point five megapixel photo, with pixels that act like two point two four micrometres. In bright daylight, the phone can use full resolution for detail. In dim light, it switches to binning. Fewer pixels, but more light each, and a much cleaner image.

scenes.chapterTitle: Your phone shoots before you press
scenes.badge: Frames already saved when you tap
scenes.sub: Google HDR+ keeps the latest 9 or 15 frames in memory
scenes.text: And the second answer is even more surprising. When your camera app is open, many phones are already capturing frames, constantly, before you press anything. Google's HDR plus system, for example, keeps the most recent nine or fifteen frames in memory. The moment you tap the shutter, it grabs those frames from just before your tap, lines them up, and stacks them into one photo. Each single frame is a little noisy, but the noise is random, so it is different in every frame. The real detail is the same in every frame. Averaging many frames together keeps the detail and cancels out much of the noise. That is why the photo you get is cleaner than any single frame the sensor captured.

scenes.chapterTitle: How night mode sees in the dark
scenes.text: Night mode takes this idea to the extreme. When Google launched Night Sight in twenty eighteen, it captured between six and fifteen frames after you pressed the shutter. If the phone was resting perfectly still, each frame could be exposed for up to one second. If you were holding it in your hand, it used shorter frames, about one fifteenth of a second or less, to avoid blur from your shaking hands. Then the software aligns all those frames, even if the phone moved a little, and merges them into one bright, clean image. That is why your phone asks you to hold still for a few seconds at night. It is not taking one photo. It is taking many and blending them.

items.text: Pixels turn light into numbers, brightness only
A colour filter plus guessing creates colour
Many frames are stacked into one photo

scenes.text: Let us recap in three points. One. The lens focuses light onto millions of tiny pixels, and each pixel turns light into a number that measures brightness only. Two. A mosaic of red, green and blue filters, plus clever guessing from neighbouring pixels, turns those colour blind numbers into a full colour image. Three. Because the pixels are so small, phones use binning and capture many frames, then stack them together to cut noise and see in the dark. So every photo on your phone is part captured, and part calculated.
